slides.title: Order of Operations with Radicals
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the prerequisite and it is the one half the room gets wrong. Multiplication and division are one level, taken as they come from the left: 12 ÷ 3 is 4 and 4 · 2 is 8. A board that answers 2 multiplied first because the multiplication sign looked more important. Say at the reveal that there is no rule anywhere that says multiply before divide.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Four levels, and the first one is the one that matters. A grouping symbol is anything that holds part of the expression together: parentheses, brackets, the radical bar from yesterday, and the fraction bar. Innermost first. Then powers and roots, which sit at the same level as each other. Then multiplying and dividing, left to right. Then adding and subtracting, left to right. Do not give the class a mnemonic — the state guide asks us not to, because a mnemonic leaves the radical bar and the fraction bar out and then students do not know where to put them.
OFF: 'There is nothing to memorise here. Read the expression, ask what is holding what, and the order tells you itself.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Two lines, and both of them undo something students believe. Multiplication does not come before division; they are one level and you take them as they come. Addition does not come before subtraction either. Write both wrong answers next to the right ones and leave them there for the whole lesson.
OFF: 'Nothing in mathematics says multiply before divide. They are the same level, and you read left to right like a sentence.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
A fraction bar is two grouping symbols at once: everything on top is finished, everything underneath is finished, and only then does the division happen. The second line is the state assessment's own item and it is worth going slowly through — under the radical, 4/9 − 1/3 is 1/9, whose root is 1/3; on the left, 3 over 36 is 1/12; and a twelfth minus a third is negative.
OFF: 'A fraction bar is a grouping symbol on the top and another one on the bottom. Finish each, then divide.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.sub: A grouping symbol inside a grouping symbol.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The state assessment's own item. Ask which piece is innermost before anything is evaluated, and make the class say 'the power' rather than point at it.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: The power is inside the parentheses, so it goes first even though it is a level below grouping — because it is inside. Then the subtraction inside, then the multiplication, then the cube root, then the addition. A board with 3.44 multiplied 4 by 8.63 first; a board with −6.44 forgot the cube root.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same shape, a square root and a positive answer. 2.1² is 4.41, and 5.4 − 4.41 is 0.99. Catches 16.2 − 4.41 (multiplied before finishing the parentheses) and 2.97 (the root forgotten).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A fraction bar and a radical in one expression.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The state assessment's other item. Ask how many grouping symbols are in it before anyone writes — there are three: the numerator, the denominator, and the radical bar.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Three groups, each finished on its own before anything crosses between them. Under the radical, 1/3 is 3/9, so the difference is 1/9. A board with 1/12 − 1/9 took the root of only one part; a board with positive 1/4 subtracted the wrong way round.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Same three groups, and both halves land on a half. 3² − 1 is 8, over 16 is 1/2; 7/16 − 3/16 is 4/16, whose root is 1/2. Catches 1/2 + 1/4 (the root never taken).

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: The warm-up question again, now with boards up, because it is the single most common order error in the course. A board with 2 multiplied 3 by 2 first.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Ruling 22's board: the diagonal is true — a 14 cm square has a diagonal of 19.80 cm — and completely unnecessary; a perimeter needs the side only. A board holding 19.8 anywhere used it; a board with 14 stopped at the side.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: The same error in the other pair of operations. A board with 3 added 4 and 3 first — and every student who does it will tell you addition comes before subtraction, which is not a rule anyone made.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: The fraction bar as two grouping symbols. A board with 8 − 5/36 − 27 divided before finishing; a board with 3/9 has the right value and has not reduced it, which is worth naming as not wrong.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. Three different errors, one per option, and each is a different level of the structure. A board full of B means Notes I's level 3 did not land.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic on the fraction bar. B and C are the same misunderstanding taken in two directions, and naming that out loud is worth more than either answer.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: The structural item of the day. In the first term the exponent is attached to the 2 and the minus sign is applied afterwards; in the second the parentheses put the minus inside the base. A board with 8 squared both as if they were the same; a board with −8 squared neither.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The state assessment's own item, and the guide accepts 51/18 without reducing. Inside the parentheses, 1/8 and 1/9 need a common denominator of 72. A board with 17/6 and a board with 51/18 are the same answer; say so.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written, and it is the exit evidence. Roscoe's sentence is very nearly right, and the difference between 'never negative' and 'always positive' is the whole item. At n = 121 the root is 11, the bracket is 0, and 0² is 0 — which is neither negative nor positive. Full credit needs the value of n and the sentence. (The radicand is a variable here, which is why this item is tagged out of the radicand scan.)

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in silence.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
